**Research note: PostgreSQL limits for schema and pool sizing**

**Identifier length.** By default PostgreSQL identifiers, such as table and column names, can be at most 63 bytes. The server uses "no more than NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes of an identifier", and NAMEDATALEN defaults to 64 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). Longer names are accepted but silently truncated. Two long names that share the first 63 bytes will therefore collide. The limit is in bytes, not characters, so multibyte UTF-8 names hit it sooner. Raising it means changing NAMEDATALEN and recompiling PostgreSQL, which is not practical on managed services. The limits page confirms the 63-byte figure (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html).

**Columns per table.** A table can have at most 1,600 columns. That ceiling is "further limited by tuple size fitting on a single page" (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Rows must fit in an 8 KB heap page, with large values moved out of line by TOAST. In practice, 1,600 `int` columns (about 6,400 bytes) fit, but 1,600 `bigint` columns do not. Dropped columns still count toward the 1,600, so a table that has had many columns added and dropped over time can run out of slots. A schema near this limit is almost always a sign to normalise or move sparse attributes into `jsonb`.

**Default max_connections.** The default is typically 100, but it can be lower if kernel settings can't support it, as determined during initdb. The parameter can only be changed at server start (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). The same page says `superuser_reserved_connections` defaults to 3. Those slots are held back for superusers, so ordinary clients effectively get about 97 by default, and fewer if `reserved_connections` is also set. Managed providers often set their own default, so check the live value with `SHOW max_connections;` rather than assuming 100.

**Caveats.** I read the "current" documentation pages, which track the latest release. The 63-byte and 1,600-column figures have been stable across versions, but I did not check older versions, and `reserved_connections` only exists in recent ones. The page I read did not give a per-connection memory cost, so I'm not making a claim about it here.

**Recommendation.** Keep identifiers well under 63 bytes, say 40 or fewer, and keep tables far below 1,600 columns. Size the application pool so the total across all service instances stays comfortably below `max_connections` minus the reserved slots, and put a pooler such as PgBouncer in front if you need more clients than that.

**Research note: PostgreSQL defaults for memory and WAL settings**

I read the official PostgreSQL documentation pages for all three settings. The "current" docs pages track the latest release.

**work_mem.** The default is 4MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The limit applies per sort or hash operation, not per query or per connection. A complex query can use several multiples of it at once, and so can many concurrent sessions. The default is conservative, so raising it globally is risky on a server with many connections.

**shared_buffers.** The default is typically 128MB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html). The docs add that it might be lower if the kernel settings can't support it, as determined during initdb. Check the value on your install with `SHOW shared_buffers;` rather than assuming 128MB. This default is small for any dedicated database server.

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1GB (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). It is a soft limit on how large the WAL can grow between automatic checkpoints. The same page gives `min_wal_size` a default of 80MB. When WAL growth hits `max_wal_size`, a checkpoint is triggered. On write-heavy systems this can cause more frequent checkpoints than you want.

**Recommendation.** Raise `shared_buffers` from the default to a sensible share of RAM for a dedicated host, and raise `max_wal_size` if the logs show checkpoints triggered by WAL volume rather than by time. Leave `work_mem` low globally and raise it per session or per role for known heavy queries.

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL, and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's configuration reference lists the default `memory_limit` (alias `max_memory`) as 80% of the system's RAM (source: https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html). The older `/docs/stable` and `/docs/current` URLs only redirect to this page. If DuckDB shares a host with PostgreSQL, 80% leaves little headroom for `shared_buffers` and backend memory. I'd set an explicit limit in that case.

**SQLite size.** The SQLite limits page gives the maximum database file size as 4294967294 pages. At the largest page size of 65536 bytes, that is about 281 terabytes (256 tebibytes) (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). The same page says the figure is about 17.5 terabytes at the default 4096-byte page size. Either way, file size is unlikely to be a constraint for a side-store.

**MERGE in PostgreSQL.** The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Add SQL MERGE command to adjust one table to match another". That makes 15 the first major version to include it (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/). The PostgreSQL 15 reference page for MERGE exists and describes it as a single statement that can conditionally INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html). That page also lists restrictions: MERGE doesn't support materialized views, foreign tables, tables with rules, or WITH RECURSIVE. So MERGE is available on 15, but not on 14 or earlier. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT on older versions.

**Recommendation.** Choose DuckDB for the analytics side-store, because SQLite's file-size limit is not a practical concern but its row-oriented engine is built for transactional use, not scans and aggregations. Cap DuckDB's memory explicitly if it runs on the PostgreSQL host. MERGE is safe to use on PostgreSQL 15 and later.

I judged the SQLite-versus-DuckDB workload fit from general knowledge, not from the pages I read.

{"answers": {"1": "80% of RAM", "2": "about 281 TB (2.8e14 bytes, at 65536-byte pages)", "3": "PostgreSQL 15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/configuration/overview.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/15.0/", "https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-merge.html"]}}

**Research note: TLS version, DNS label length and the 418 status code**

**1. TLS 1.3.** The RFC that has specified TLS 1.3 since 2018 is RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3" (August 2018, Proposed Standard). Its abstract says "This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). The RFC Editor page now marks RFC 8446 as obsolete. The replacement is RFC 9846, which has the same title. It says it "obsoletes RFC 8446, which specified TLS 1.3" and also obsoletes RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). RFC 9846 describes itself as a minor, backward-compatible update that keeps the version number. RFC 8446 is still the number most older documents cite. The current reference is RFC 9846. I read only the first 100,000 characters of each of these pages, which was enough for the title, status and obsoletes statements.

**2. DNS label length.** RFC 1035 says "Labels must be 63 characters or less" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The wire format stores a label as a length octet followed by that many octets, so the limit is 63 octets. For ASCII host names, characters and octets are the same. Internationalised names count in their encoded (punycode) form. I did not read the part of the page covering the total-name limit. RFC 1035 sets that at 255 octets in wire format. That is a separate limit, and I am quoting it from memory, not from this lookup.

**3. "I'm a teapot".** The status code is 418. It is defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)" (Informational, dated 1 April 1998). Section 2.3.2 says: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code '418 I'm a teapot'" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). The page labels it as humor, and it is not an Internet standard. It notes that RFC 7168 updated it.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 as the current TLS 1.3 specification, and mention RFC 8446 as its predecessor so older references still make sense. State the DNS label limit as 63 octets, and treat 418 as a non-standard, joke status code that production services shouldn't depend on.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, Aug 2018); now obsoleted by RFC 9846", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418, defined in RFC 2324"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: default limits for the deploy runbook**

**Lambda timeout.** One invocation can be configured for at most 900 seconds (15 minutes). The default is 3 seconds, adjustable in 1-second steps (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page says Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 5,400 seconds for asynchronous invocations and for event source mappings, with Amazon MQ and Amazon DocumentDB excluded. Standard functions are capped at 900 seconds, so use that for the runbook unless the service runs on Managed Instances.

**Kubernetes grace period.** A Pod gets 30 seconds to terminate gracefully by default. The page says "A Pod is granted a term to terminate gracefully, which defaults to 30 seconds," and that the default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is 30 (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). After that window the kubelet force-kills the container with SIGKILL. Any shutdown or drain step in the runbook has to finish inside 30 seconds, or the Pod spec has to override the value.

**Docker default bridge.** I could not find an official Docker page that states docker0's default subnet outright, so this answer is inferred. The bridge-driver page shows containers on the default bridge at 172.17.0.2 and 172.17.0.3, with `inet 172.17.0.2/16` in the `ip addr` output, which implies 172.17.0.0/16 (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/). Docker's networking page lists a default address pool whose first entry is `{ "base": "172.17.0.0/16", "size": 16 }` (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). That is consistent with the inference, but neither page links the range to docker0 in words. The bridge page also shows that `bip` in `daemon.json` can override the subnet, for example to 192.168.1.0/24 in its example. Treat 172.17.0.0/16 as the default, and check it on the actual host with `docker network inspect bridge` before relying on it.

**Recommendation.** Write the runbook around the shortest of these limits: shutdown must finish within 30 seconds on Kubernetes, and a single Lambda run must finish within 900 seconds. Also confirm the docker0 subnet on each local host, because a 172.17.0.0/16 conflict with a VPN or corporate network is a common cause of local networking problems.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16 (inferred from Docker examples; not stated outright)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": ["https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/drivers/bridge/", "https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/"]}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** The default `testTimeout` is 5,000 ms (5 seconds) when tests run in Node. It rises to 15,000 ms if `browser.enabled` is true (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). The team's config only needs an override if it runs browser mode or has slow integration tests.

**Rust in the Linux kernel.** Linux 6.1 was the first mainline release with Rust support. The KernelNewbies page for that release says: "This release adds support for the Rust programming language." It also calls the support preliminary: "This release includes some initial support for Rust, which will be improved in later releases." (source: https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1). I did not check the kernel.org release announcement or the in-tree documentation. I also read only the first 100,000 of the page's roughly 239,000 characters, which was enough to find the statement. If the team follows a kernel version for Rust, 6.1 is the earliest possible floor. In practice the Rust support was still minimal then, so a newer kernel would be the sensible baseline.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout. The PostgreSQL documentation says: "A value of zero (the default) disables the timeout." A value given without units is read as milliseconds (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). That page is the "current" docs, so the default could change in a later major version. Any limit therefore has to be set explicitly, either per role, per database or per session.

**Recommendation.** Keep vitest's 5 s default for unit tests and raise it only for specific slow suites, and set an explicit PostgreSQL `statement_timeout` (for example per application role), because the default allows queries to run forever. Treat Linux 6.1 as the earliest kernel with Rust support, but pick the team's target kernel from current Rust-for-Linux guidance rather than from that first release.

{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms (15000 ms in browser mode)", "2": "Linux 6.1", "3": "0 (disabled, no timeout)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.1"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html"]}}
